title: Three kinds of reading
hook: unbroken, continuous, and the slow sehaj path at your own pace

segments.voice: Yesterday, taking the hukam: one hymn, received and not chosen, from the top of the left-hand page. Your line was the order of the day. What did your line say about the hours that followed? Day one thousand two hundred sixty.

A long book can be read the way a marathon is run, or the way a garden is walked. Some people sprint the last chapters at two in the morning because they can't stop. Others leave a bookmark in for a season and come back to it on Sundays. Both finish. They just meet different books along the way. Yesterday, the hukam gave one hymn for one day. Today the question gets bigger: how do Sikhs read the whole Guru Granth Sahib, from its first page to its last? There's more than one pace for it, and each one has a name.
screen: `A MARATHON, OR A GARDEN WALK.` → `FROM ONE HYMN TO THE WHOLE GRANTH.` → `MORE THAN ONE PACE.`

segments.voice: A path, in Punjabi, is a reading. The first pace is the akhand path. Akhand means unbroken. The whole Granth is read aloud from start to finish without a single pause, by a team of readers taking turns, one handing the line to the next so the voice never stops. Families hold one for a wedding, a birth, a death, a new house, or a hard time. The code speaks to how it should be done: clearly, carefully, with attention, never as a background noise. The second pace keeps the reading going in order across set sittings, day after day, so that it finishes in time for an occasion. Continuous, but with rests. And the third is the sehaj path. It has no clock at all. You read the Granth in order, at your own pace, a page or a hymn at a sitting, and you pick up where you stopped. It can be done by one person alone at home, in whatever time life allows. Now the word sehaj. In Gurbani it names poise, ease, a settled balance of the mind, the calm that comes when a person stops fighting the hukam. So the slow reading is named for the state it hopes to grow. You don't read the Granth fast in order to reach sehaj. You read it in sehaj. That's a fitting place to land the week. It began with rising early, then the sangat, the gurdwara's order, the Granth opened and rested, the words that may be sung, the hukam. Each one was about how the word is received. The sehaj path says it can be received at a walking pace too. Your own pace.
screen: `PATH: A READING.` · `AKHAND: UNBROKEN, READERS IN TURN.` · `IN ORDER, WITH RESTS, OR WITH NO CLOCK.` · `SEHAJ: POISE, A SETTLED EASE.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a slow reading. Settle, and breathe. Choose a text that matters to you, the Granth, if it's yours, or any book you've always meant to read properly. Now be honest about your days. How much could you read at one sitting without rushing? A page? A hymn? A paragraph? Where would you sit, and when? Picture the bookmark going in at the end of the first sitting. Then rest, without hurrying toward anything, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Sehaj path. A reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, in order, at your own pace, named for sehaj, poise and settled ease. Today's word.
Your line: your own pace. Today, read one page of something that matters, slowly, and put a bookmark in where you stopped. Day one thousand two hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Sikh families arrange an akhand path, read without a break by a team of readers, for weddings, births, deaths and other occasions; others keep a sehaj path at home, reading the Granth in order at their own pace.

fork.setup: you want to read the whole Granth, but you have a job, a family and a few quiet minutes a day. which reading fits?
options: an akhand path, alone, without stopping.
a sehaj path, in order, at your own pace.
none; wait until life is quieter.
fork.reveal: the sehaj path is made for this: one person, in order, as much as a sitting allows, picking up where you stopped.

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one way to read the Granth: fast, start to finish.
what it means: Sikhs read it unbroken in the akhand path, with rests across set sittings, or slowly in the sehaj path.
what a scholar hears: sehaj is Gurbani's word for poise, so the slow reading is named for the state it hopes to grow.
